newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SBC sees Swiss move to neutral money policy in '97.
newsitem.headline: SBC sees Swiss move to neutral money policy in '97.

text.p: Swiss Bank Corp's top economist said he thought the Swiss National Bank (SNB) would shift its expansive monetary policy to a more neutral stance in the course of this year to head off inflationary pressure.

The SNB has already laid the monetary groundwork for an economic recovery by adopting an expansive policy since 1995 and would only fuel inflation by pumping more liquidity into the system, Group Economist Klaus Wellershoff told reporters.

"It is clear that while the National Bank's expansive policy is necessary at the moment, at some time in the course of the year it must take its foot off the accelerator and move to a more neutral policy position," he said.

His comment contrasted sharply with the view of Credit Suisse First Boston, which said yesterday that the SNB would become even more expansive on news that unemployment hit a record 5.7 percent in January, underscoring economic weakness.
CSFB said unemployment would continue to rise steeply in months to come, hitting six percent by March and showing GDP fell in the last quarter of 1996 and the first quarter of 1997.

"The deep crisis in Switzerland will become an issue and a complete redefinition of monetary and fiscal policies is increasingly likely. So be prepared, over the remainder of the year, for a Japanese-like easing of monetary policy," it said.
"The Swiss franc will soon weaken in a big way."
An SNB spokesman said the central bank would not react to every comment by economists.

He reiterated the central bank still stood by the position it laid out in December that it would remain generous until there were clear signs that the economy, which has basically stagnated since 1990, was picking up.

Wellershoff did not say when a shift was likely, but added the SNB was keeping its eye out for the first signs of economic recovery and would send clear signals to markets when it thought the time was ripe to start adjusting policy.

"You don't have to be a monetarist to have some fear of inflation," Wellershoff said, noting the last time M1 money supply grew at such a rate, in 1987, it led to six percent inflation in the early 1990s.

"We are not so naive as to forecast six percent inflation," he said, citing structural adjustments, increased competition and a different labour market situation as good reasons prices will not rise as much now.
"But from this point of view we cannot assume that inflation will remain below one percent in Switzerland in years to come," he said.

Wellershoff interpreted recent statements from SNB officials that the consumer price index overstates inflation as a sign that the central bank was preparing public opinion for a period of higher inflation.
"Don't get me wrong," he added. "If we now define price stability as two percent inflation, then we could live with this very well."
Wellershoff said he would not rule out the dollar's advance to 1.50 francs, but said purchasing power parity considerations argued for a stronger Swiss franc in the longer term.
